blocks.text: **The task.** Reverse an array of characters in place. Return nothing — modify the input array itself, using O(1) extra memory.

The obvious solution builds a new array by reading the input backwards. That works, but it costs O(N) extra space — and the problem explicitly forbids it. So the reversal has to happen by moving elements *within* the array we already have.
Notice what reversing actually does to positions. The first element ends up last, the second ends up second-to-last, and so on. Every element swaps with its mirror across the centre.
So pair up the mirrors and swap each pair. Two pointers at the ends give exactly those pairs.

blocks.code:
['h','e','l','l','o']    left=0 right=4  swap h,o
['o','e','l','l','h']    left=1 right=3  swap e,l
['o','l','l','e','h']    left=2 right=2  stop

blocks.text: The loop stops when both pointers reach index 2. That middle character is already where it belongs — in an odd-length array the centre never moves.
**Time: O(N)** — N/2 iterations, each doing constant work.
**Space: O(1)** — two integers and a swap. Nothing grows with the input.
